A 20-year-old male with type 1 diabetes mellitus arrives at the emergency department 35 minutes after
sustaining a gunshot wound to his right thigh. His vital signs show: pulse 101/min, respirations 17/min,
blood pressure 100/76 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination reveals
an entrance wound on the anteromedial right thigh, 2 cm inferior to the inguinal ligament, with no exit
wound or active bleeding. There is no bruit or thrill on auscultation, though the right pedal pulse is
diminished compared to the left. The abdomen is soft and nontender, with no other abnormal findings.
Laboratory results show: | Hematocrit | 46% | | --- | --- | | Serum | | | Urea nitrogen | 24 mg/dL | | Glucose
| 160 mg/dL | | Creatinine | 3.1 mg/dL | What is the most appropriate first step in management? Answer
Choices: (A) Intravenous heparin administration (B) Observation with serial physical exams (C)
Arteriography with catheter-based intervention (D) CT angiography (E) Magnetic resonance
angiography (F) Surgical exploration (G) Fasciotomy (H) Duplex ultrasonography (I) Measurement of
ankle-brachial index (J) Plain radiography of the thigh
 A. Fasciotomy
